**bones 0.2.0 is on CRAN.** CRAN accepted it on 13 November. It is the
first update since [bones went on CRAN](../2026-10-26-bones-on-cran/index.qmd)
in October.

bones gives a Shiny output a loading placeholder in the shape of its
content. You wrap the output, and that is all:

```r
withBones(tableOutput("results"))
```

Until now, the shape was a guess. bones read the type of the output, a
table here, and drew a table of six rows. Most of this release came from
one question: why guess, when the browser has seen the real content?

## A skeleton that learns the page

An output now learns the shape of its content. After a load, the browser
records where each line of text, each image and each card is. On the next
visit, the first skeleton has that shape, not the guess.

The first visit still shows the built-in shape. From the second visit, a
table of three narrow columns looks like a table of three narrow columns,
and a summary card looks like that card.

It is on by default, with some limits:

- **It stores only numbers.** The record holds the place and the size of
  each box, never the text. It is kept in the browser of the user, in
  `localStorage`, for that page and that output.
- **It needs almost the same width.** A record from a wide window is not
  used in a narrow one. The skeleton then has the built-in shape.
- **You can still name the shape.** When you give `type`, `rows`, `cols`,
  `lines`, `n` or `skeleton`, bones uses what you gave. Charts do not
  learn either: their shape comes from the chart type.

To turn it off for one output, or for the whole app:

```r
withBones(tableOutput("results"), learn = FALSE)
bones_defaults(learn = FALSE)
```

`remember = FALSE` turns off both the remembered height and the learned
shape.

### What counts as a card

The hard part was not to measure the page. It was to decide what to keep.

Text is easy: each line of text becomes a bar. An image, a canvas or an
input also becomes a bar. A card is harder. bones calls an element a
frame if it has a border on all four sides, or a background of its own.
A frame is drawn behind the bars in it.

That rule found many false cards before it worked:

- A striped table row has its own background. It is not a card. bones
  skips the parts of a table, in a `<table>` and in a table made of
  `<div>` elements with ARIA roles, as reactable makes.
- A button has a background too. It is a bar already.
- A clear background can be written `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)` or
  `color(srgb 1 0 0 / 0)`. Both are clear.
- A box that scrolls hides rows under its edge. bones records only what
  shows.

One more rule: when one box covers most of the content, such as a map or a
big canvas, nothing is stored. A single grey block gives no useful shape.

## When an output fails

A failed output now shows a calm panel in place of the red error text of
Shiny:

```r
withBones(plotOutput("chart"), error = bones_error("The chart could not be loaded."))
```

`bones_error()` with no message says "This content could not be loaded."
After a good load, the old content stays on the screen, dimmed, and the
panel sits over it as a banner. The user keeps what they were reading.

**This is a change of behaviour.** The panel is on by default, so an app
that updates to 0.2.0 shows it at once. To keep the error text of Shiny:

```r
bones_defaults(error = FALSE)
```

A silent `req()` and a `validate()` message are not errors. They keep
their usual behaviour.

The raw error message stays hidden by default. `bones_error(detail = TRUE)`
shows it under the panel. Use that in development only: a raw error can
hold file paths, SQL or private data. A message from `safeError()` still
shows, because you wrote it for the user.

### Try again

Give `retry` an input id, and the panel gets a "Try again" button:

```r
withBones(plotOutput("chart"), retry = "chart_retry")

output$chart <- renderPlot({
  input$chart_retry
  make_chart(data())
})
```

The button sets the input, and shows the skeleton while the output runs
again. The output reads the input, so a click runs it again. bones does
not run anything itself. That keeps the retry in the code of the app,
where you can see it.

## A skeleton before the output starts

Sometimes an app does work before it updates an output. The user clicks
"Refresh", the server fetches data for a second, and only then does the
output start. For that second, the old content stayed on the screen, as if
nothing had happened.

`hold` shows the skeleton as soon as an input changes:

```r
withBones(textOutput("result"), hold = "refresh")
```

The skeleton keeps the space of the content, and the content comes back
when the output has its new value.

There is one case `hold` cannot cover. If the output changes later, after
`later::later()` or a poll, Shiny is idle in the gap. bones lets a hold go
at idle, so that a hold that never gets a value does not stay forever.
For that case, start the hold from JavaScript:

```js
Bones.hold("result");     // shows the skeleton until the next value
Bones.release("result");  // or until you end it
```

I chose a pair of verbs over one function with a flag, such as
`Bones.hold(el, false)`. `Bones.release()` says what it does. A second
argument to `Bones.hold()` now gives a warning in the console, so the old
form does not fail in silence.

## Colours from CSS

The colours of a skeleton come from the theme. With a bslib theme, the
bars take a faint tint of the text colour, and they turn light in a dark
theme.

An app with its own CSS can now set them too, with or without Bootstrap:

```css
:root {
  --bones-text: #1d3557;
  --bones-surface: #ffffff;
  --bones-radius: 6px;
}

.dark-panel {
  --bones-text: #f1faee;
  --bones-surface: #1d3557;
}
```

`--bones-text` is the colour that the bars are made from. `--bones-surface`
is the background of the page. `--bones-color`, `--bones-highlight` and the
others set one colour each.

These properties existed before, but a value on `:root` did nothing. The
reason was in my own stylesheet. bones declared `--bones-color` on each
wrapper, so that each part of a page follows its own theme, such as a dark
card on a light page. A custom property declared on an element is
stronger than the value that it gets from its parent. My value on the
wrapper won every time.

The fix uses two sets of names. bones only reads `--bones-color` and the
other public names, and never declares them. It computes its own private
values, `--_bones-color` and the others, on each wrapper. Your value can
then sit anywhere above the wrapper, and each part of the page still
follows its own theme.

If you publish CSS custom properties for other people to set, do not
declare them yourself on the element that uses them. Read them, and keep
your own values under other names.

## A strict Content-Security-Policy

bones now works on a page whose policy blocks inline styles, such as
`style-src 'self'` with no `'unsafe-inline'`. Such a policy blocks every
`style` attribute, and bones used them for the size of each bar.

bones now writes the sizes into a `data-bones-style` attribute. Its script
sets them in the browser, through the style object of each element, which
the policy allows. The look does not change.

## The smaller things

- **Names must match exactly.** `type = "pi"` used to work, as a short
  form of `"pie"`. It is now an error that says `Did you mean "pie"?`. The
  same applies to `animation` and to the `shape` of `bones_block()`. A
  short form could break the day a new name started with the same letters.
- **An unused shape argument gives a warning.** `withBones(plotOutput("x"),
  rows = 8)` passed `rows` to a chart, which has no rows, and said nothing.
  `bones_auto()` does not give these warnings, because it passes the same
  arguments to every output.
- **`bones_shapes()` and `bones_animations()`** list the valid names.
- **`speed` and `color`** now work on one output, as well as for the whole
  app: `withBones(plotOutput("chart"), speed = 0.8, color = "#dbeafe")`.
- **`bones_defaults()` with no arguments** returns the current values. The
  signature of `withBones()` now shows the session options as its
  defaults, so you can see where each default comes from.
- **A custom skeleton keeps its own height.** It used to reserve the height
  that bones guessed for the type of the output.
- **`stale = FALSE` no longer flashes a blank box.** The old content now
  stays until the skeleton appears.
- **A misspelt argument of `bones_auto()`** gives a short error, with a
  hint for the name you meant.

## Try it

```r
install.packages("bones")
```
